topic: Physics — National and global energy resources
subject: combined-science

items.q: A student is asked to list the main energy resources available for use on Earth. Which list is correct?
items.correct: Nuclear fuel, the tides, geothermal energy and water waves
items.misconception: Bio-fuel, wind, hydro-electricity and mains electricity
items.why: Electricity arrives at a socket like a supply, and students meet 'electrical energy' constantly, so it feels like a source. Trace it back one step: every unit of electricity came from a resource on the specification's list.
items.random_wrong: Coal, oil, gas and the steam produced in a boiler

items.q: Where does the energy supplied by a geothermal resource come from?
items.correct: From the hot rock lying deep below the Earth's surface
items.misconception: From sunlight that has warmed the ground during the day
items.why: Students know the Sun warms the ground and reason that all underground warmth must have the same origin. Geothermal wells reach rock that is hot far below the depth sunlight has any effect on.
items.random_wrong: From fossil fuels that are burning deep underground

items.q: Which statement is the specification's definition of a renewable energy resource?
items.correct: One that is being, or can be, replenished as it is used
items.misconception: One with a supply so large that it could never all be used up
items.why: The everyday word suggests endlessness, and students meet it alongside slogans such as 'the wind will always blow'. The specification's test is replacement, not size. Bio-fuel is renewable only because the crops are grown again; stop replanting and it runs out.
items.random_wrong: One that gives off no carbon dioxide while it is being used

items.q: Nuclear fuel is classified as non-renewable. Which reason for that classification is correct?
items.correct: The uranium used is not replenished as it is used
items.misconception: Uranium is mined from rock, so it is a fossil fuel
items.why: 'Mined from rock' is taken as the definition of a fossil fuel instead of 'formed from the remains of living things'. Both are non-renewable, but for the classification question the list of fossil fuels is fixed at three.
items.random_wrong: Nuclear power stations release carbon dioxide as they run

items.q: Why is bio-fuel classified as a renewable energy resource?
items.correct: The crops it is made from can be grown again as the fuel is used
items.misconception: It gives off much less carbon dioxide than burning coal does
items.why: Renewables are advertised as the green choice, so students merge 'clean' and 'renewable' into one category. Ask only one question: is it being replenished as it is used? Answer that first, then treat environmental impact as a separate judgement.
items.random_wrong: There is so much plant material that it could never run out

items.q: New coal is still slowly forming underground today. Why is coal still classed as non-renewable?
items.correct: New coal is forming far more slowly than it is being used
items.misconception: It is not: coal is renewable because new coal is still forming
items.why: The word 'replenished' is read as 'any replacement at all', with no attention to rate. Replenishment has to keep pace with use. Coal takes millions of years to form and is burned in a moment.
items.random_wrong: Coal gives off carbon dioxide, and renewables are clean

items.q: The specification gives three uses of energy resources. Which set of three is correct?
items.correct: Transport, electricity generation and heating
items.misconception: Transport, electricity generation and lighting
items.why: Students substitute familiar household jobs for the specification's broader categories. Lighting and cooking sit inside the listed categories - they are things done with electricity or with heating.
items.random_wrong: Electricity generation, heating and cooking food

items.q: Which energy resource supplies most of the energy used for transport worldwide?
items.correct: Oil, as petrol and diesel
items.misconception: Electricity from wind farms
items.why: Nothing is burned at the car, so the impact of generating the electricity is invisible to the user. Follow the chain back to the power station: the resource used is the one that made the electricity.

items.q: Panels on the roof of a house use the Sun to warm the water in a hot water tank. Which use of an energy resource is this?
items.correct: Heating, because the Sun's energy is warming the water directly
items.misconception: Electricity generation, because solar panels make electricity
items.why: 'Solar panel' is used loosely for two different things, and electricity is the use students hear about. Ask what comes out: hot water means the use is heating; a supply to the mains means electricity generation.
items.random_wrong: Transport, because that is a common use of energy

items.q: Which group of resources is used for all three of transport, electricity generation and heating?
items.correct: Fossil fuels, which are burned for all three of these jobs
items.misconception: Wind, which could drive vehicles, power stations and radiators
items.why: The idea that energy can be transferred in many ways is over-generalised into 'every resource suits every job'. Compare actual uses. You cannot run a lorry off a tidal stream, and nobody heats a house with uranium.
items.random_wrong: The tides, which run at all hours and serve every use

items.q: Why is a wind farm a less reliable energy resource than a gas-fired power station?
items.correct: Its output falls when the wind drops, whatever the demand
items.misconception: It is not less reliable, because the wind never stops blowing
items.why: Everyday experience of breezy days, plus the fact that turbines are often turning, hides the calm periods. Reliability means available when it is wanted. A calm, cold evening is exactly when demand is high and wind output is low.
items.random_wrong: Each turbine gives out less energy than a gas power station

items.q: Tidal energy is described as a reliable energy resource. Which statement explains why?
items.correct: The tides rise and fall on a known cycle
items.misconception: The tides are driven by winds that blow daily
items.why: Waves and tides are both movements of the sea and get merged into one idea. Tide tables are printed years ahead. That predictability is exactly why tidal energy counts as reliable.
items.random_wrong: Tidal stations give out more energy than any other

items.q: Which environmental impact arises directly from burning fossil fuels in a power station?
items.correct: Carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide are released into the air
items.misconception: Radioactive waste is produced and has to be stored safely
items.why: 'Mined from rock' is taken as the definition of a fossil fuel instead of 'formed from the remains of living things'. Both are non-renewable, but for the classification question the list of fossil fuels is fixed at three.
items.random_wrong: The steam from the cooling towers poisons nearby land

items.q: Which statement about the environmental impact of renewable energy resources is correct?
items.correct: They have impacts too, such as land flooded behind a hydro dam
items.misconception: They cause no environmental damage of any kind at all
items.why: Renewables are presented as the solution to pollution, and 'less impact' is heard as 'no impact'. Ask what had to be built or grown, and what land was used, before deciding a resource is harmless.
items.random_wrong: Bio-fuel is the one renewable that has no effect at all on land use

items.q: The share of UK electricity generated from renewable resources has risen sharply since 2010. Which explanation of this trend is best?
items.correct: Concern about carbon dioxide, and cheaper wind and solar
items.misconception: The UK's coal, oil and gas have now all been used up
items.why: 'Non-renewable' is heard as 'about to run out', so scarcity is assumed to be the driver. Known reserves are still large. It is impact and cost, not exhaustion, that explain the recent trend.
items.random_wrong: Renewables can now supply power at all times without any backup

items.q: Scientists identified the harm caused by burning fossil fuels many years ago, yet their use has continued. Which statement best explains this?
items.correct: Political, social, ethical and economic factors count too
items.misconception: The evidence is still too uncertain for anyone to act on it
items.why: School science is presented as a sequence of problems solved, so identifying and solving look like the same step. Cost, jobs, public opinion and international agreement all decide what is actually done with what science has shown.
items.random_wrong: Scientists have not yet explained the harm to any government

items.q: Does renewable mean the energy is free?
items.correct: Renewable describes replenishment, not price. Wind farms and dams cost a great deal to build.
items.misconception: A renewable resource costs nothing, because nobody has to pay for the wind or the sunlight.
items.why: Students hear that the fuel is free and generalise it to the whole resource. Separate the fuel cost from the classification. The definition says nothing about money.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a wind turbine an energy resource?
items.correct: The resource is the wind; the turbine is the equipment used to make use of it.
items.misconception: Wind turbines, solar panels and dams are themselves energy resources.
items.why: The machinery is the visible thing, so students name the hardware rather than the supply it draws on. Name the supply, not the device: wind, the Sun, stored water.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does geothermal energy come from burning something underground?
items.correct: Nothing is burned. The rock underground is already hot, and that is the resource.
items.misconception: Geothermal energy comes from fuel burning deep inside the Earth.
items.why: Students associate 'energy from the ground' with coal, oil and gas, which do come from underground. Geothermal is renewable precisely because there is no fuel being consumed.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do nuclear power stations release carbon dioxide as they run?
items.correct: They do not burn a fuel, so no carbon dioxide is released; their characteristic impact is radioactive waste.
items.misconception: Nuclear stations pour clouds out of huge towers, so they must be releasing carbon dioxide.
items.why: The cooling-tower plume looks like smoke; it is condensed water vapour. Match each impact to its cause: carbon dioxide comes from burning, radioactive waste comes from nuclear fuel.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is bio-fuel non-renewable because burning it gives off carbon dioxide?
items.correct: Bio-fuel is renewable, because the crops it is made from can be grown again as the fuel is used.
items.misconception: Anything made from plants or other living things must be renewable, because it has a natural, living origin.
items.why: Students classify by what happens at the moment of use rather than by whether the supply is replaced. Apply the definition to the supply, not to the exhaust. New crops replace the fuel; new coal does not.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does reliable mean the resource gives out a lot of energy?
items.correct: Reliability is about availability on demand, not about output. A small geothermal plant is reliable; a huge wind farm is not.
items.misconception: The reliable resources are the powerful ones that supply the most energy.
items.why: 'Reliable' is treated as a general word of praise and merged with 'big' or 'good'. Judge reliability by one question only: can it supply energy whenever it is wanted?
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are wind and solar unreliable because the equipment breaks down?
items.correct: They are unreliable because the wind and the sunshine vary, not because the machinery is faulty.
items.misconception: Turbines and panels are badly made and keep failing, which is why they are called unreliable.
items.why: 'Unreliable' in everyday speech means 'keeps going wrong', so the fault is placed on the hardware. The turbine works perfectly on a calm day; there is simply no wind for it to use.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does carbon dioxide cause acid rain?
items.correct: Acid rain comes mainly from sulfur dioxide released when fuels containing sulfur are burned.
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide is the pollutant from burning fuels, so it must cause acid rain as well.
items.why: Carbon dioxide is the only combustion product many students can name, so it is blamed for every effect. Keep the two apart: carbon dioxide contributes to global warming; sulfur dioxide causes acid rain.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Have wind and solar already replaced fossil fuels?
items.correct: Fossil fuels still supply most of the world's energy, especially for transport and heating.
items.misconception: Renewables have taken over, so fossil fuels are basically finished as an energy resource.
items.why: Rapid growth in renewable electricity is reported constantly, and electricity is mistaken for all energy use. Separate the trend from the total: a fast-growing share can still be a small share.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
